newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian LNG plant ahead of target, 40 pct done.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian LNG plant ahead of target, 40 pct done.

text.p: Nigeria's $4 billion liquefied natural gas (LNG) project is now 40 percent completed, according to Steve Ollereanshaw, the chief executive of operator Nigeria LNG Ltd said.

"The overall engineering, procurement and construction of the project is now about 40 percent complete which is slightly ahead of schedule," he told reporters on a tour of the project site on Bonny island in the oil-producing Rivers state this week.
The project, scheduled to come on stream in October, 1999, has suffered a series of postponements in the past but Nigeria's present military government has shown more commitment to it.

"We have the incentives to complete the project on time," Ollereanshaw said, adding "The Nigerian government has put in a lot of money, we are earning interest on funds placed in escrow accounts all of which we can draw down upon. So there is no problem about financing."
The four shareholders in the project -- state oil firm Nigerian National Petreoleum Corp, Shell Sas BV, Elf Aquitaine and Agip SpA have placed $2.873 billion in escrow accounts.
Four of the Nigerian LNG ships placed on time charter to the Far East since 1992 have earned more than $250 million.
The project is to produce 7.5 billion cubic metres of gas annually for delivery to customers in Spain, France and Turkey.
The fourth and biggest buyer Enel of Italy terminated the contract last December and the issue is now before an arbitration panel.
"The arbitration process is still on in Switzerland," said Ollereanshaw, adding that the NLNG Ltd was now preparing its response to the defence submitted by Enel to the panel.
"We have not submitted claims for damages yet. The first step is to establish where the liabilities lie and this will be determined by the first quarter of 1998," he said.
Ollereanshaw said he had received proposals from Enel on its options to receive the Nigerian gas.
"But we have a three-pronged approach to the Enel issue, namely pursuit of the arbitration, evaluate Enel's proposals and offering its volume to other buyers."
There are plans to raise the LNG project from two to three trains. "The likelihood is that there will be a third train early next century," Ollereanshaw said.
"We got the approval from our board last week for detailed studies on the expansion of the plant. We will be looking at all aspects including technical, marketing and financing," he said.
The third train is expected to raise the LNG's output to between 11 and 12 billion cubic metres yearly and generate an income of $1.5 billion annually.
"Expanding the plant will mean mopping up more associated gas and elimination of gas flaring," Ollereanshaw said.
